Data Acquisition Blog
text: I am a massive fan of fighting games, and I often find myself looking at online wikis that cover different characters’ strategies as well as their “frame data” (more on that later). I play multiple different fighting games (such as Street Fighter and Smash Bros.), but the series that I want to focus on for the sake of this project is called “Guilty Gear”. This series has gathered quite a large fan base since the release of its latest game, Guilty Gear -Strive-, and has seen thousands of fans register to play in several differentt official tournaments. However, some long-time Guilty Gear fans claim that the old games are better because Guilty Gear -Strive- has simplified the many of mechanics present in older Guilty Gear games. Although game balance is an incredibly difficult subject to understand, I thought I could try to approach this discussion by acquiring some data regarding the differences in “frame data” between the two games to see if any significant trends emerge between the two games!

I play multiple different fighting games (such as Street Fighter and Smash Bros.), but the series that I want to focus on for the sake of this project is called “Guilty Gear”. This series has gathered quite a large fan base since the release of its latest game, Guilty Gear -Strive-, and has seen thousands of fans register to play in several differentt official tournaments. However, some long-time Guilty Gear fans claim that the old games are better because Guilty Gear -Strive- has simplified the many of mechanics present in older Guilty Gear games. Although game balance is an incredibly difficult subject to understand, I thought I could try to approach this discussion by acquiring some data regarding the differences in “frame data” between the two games to see if any significant trends emerge between the two games!

title: Data Acquisition Blog
text:
Motivating question

Context
For the sake of this blog, there are a few important things to understand about the attacks in this series. 1. Characters in Guilty Gear have 5 attack buttons: Punch (P), Kick (K), Slash (S), Heavy Slash (H), and Dust (D). Characters have different variations of these if they are standing, crouching, close to the opponent, or holding the button down (only in the case of Dusts in Strive) 2. Players of these games refer to the attacks that characters have in “numpad notation,” which can be unintuitive. However, this blog will mostly only cover standing attacks (denoted as 5P, 5K, etc.), crouching attacks (denoted by 2P, 2K, etc.), and close/far attacks (denoted by c.S and f.S). 3. “Frame Data” refers to how many 1/60 second “frames” it takes for a certain attack to start, stop, etc. (this comes from the games running at 60 frames per second). For instance, if an attack has “20 frame startup”, that means a third of a second will pass between the attack button being pressed and the attack actually being able to hit the enemy. 4. There are three significant attack properties discussed in the blog, which are startup (how fast an attack becomes active), recovery (effectively how long an attack’s cooldown is), and advantage on block (how much sooner you can act before an opponent after hitting their block with a given attack). These are all in terms of frames, though block advantage is positive or negative depending on whether you can act before your opponent exits blockstun or afterwards. 5. Some attacks hit low, which means that the opponent must be crouching and blocking to not get hit by the attack, and some attacks hit high, which means the the opponent must be standing and blocking to not get hit. If an attack doesn’t hit high or low, the opponent can crouch or stand while blocking. – Low attacks tend to be faster than high attacks, and generally the opponent will be crouch blocking if they are on defense.


Questions
To gauge if Strive is more simplified than past Guilty Gear games, my goal is to look into how much attacks favor the attacker in terms of frame data between the two games. Key indicators that I will look out for include: - How fast attacks generally are to start up (faster attacks can make it easier to start your offense) - How fast High attacks tend to be (Faster highs are harder to react to and make better mixups) - How much recovery moves tend to have (more recovery means that enemies can punish missed attacks more easily) - How advantageous moves tend to be on block (having positive frame advantage on the opponent’s block means that it is harder for them to challenge your offense)

title: A Beginner’s Guide to Understanding Neural Networks
text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is proving to be a an increasingly powerful tool, and some think that it is utterly inscrutable. However, I want to push back against that idea by teaching you about neural networks! Neural networks are the foundation of deep learning, so an understanding of neural networks can improve our understanding of AI! In this blog, I aim to teach the fundamentals of the structure of neural networks, how they’re trained, and give an example of neural networks running.

title: A Beginner’s Guide to Understanding Neural Networks
text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is proving to be a an increasingly powerful tool, and some think that it is utterly inscrutable. However, I want to push back against that idea by teaching you about neural networks! Neural networks are the foundation of deep learning, so an understanding of neural networks can improve our understanding of AI! In this blog, I aim to teach the fundamentals of the structure of neural networks, how they’re trained, and give an example of neural networks running.

title: A Beginner’s Guide to Understanding Neural Networks
text:
Basic Structure
A neural network’s goal is to iteratively create a function that maps existing input x’s onto correct output y’s such that we can accurately predict y’s given new x’s.

Neurons



A basic neural network


A neural network consists of a series of neurons (also called nodes) arranged in multiple interconnected layers, as shown in the above image. A given neuron works by:

taking all of the previous inputs (x1 through xn),
multiplying them by a weight (w1 through wn),
summing them (z),
adding a “bias” (b) to z,
then passing it through a nonlinearity function (𝜎⁡) .

With all of that together, the math for a given neuron’s activation a will look like this: (Note that z looks remarkably similar to a linear regression equation.) \[
z = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2+...+w_nx_n+b,\space\space a=\sigma(z)
\]
The reason we pass z into a nonlinearity function is because nonlinear functions have some bend to them, which we can transform to make the model fit the shape of the data incredibly well. If not for our nonlinearity function, a given neuron would only be able to produce a straight line and would miss out on a lot of higher level details.



Example of nonlinearity in action


Commonly used functions are this are ReLUs (which has a bend from excluding negative values) and Sigmoids (which condenses inputs to be between 0 and 1)


Layers in Neural Networks
A neural network functions by having every neuron in a given layer interact with every neuron in the next layer. The first layer is called the “input layer,” and will have a node for every input you pass into the neural network (inputs can range from various medical variables such as BMI and heart rate to pixels from an image).
From there, every input neuron will connect with every node in the next “hidden layer.” These nodes that aim to discover high-dimensional connections about the data though applying weights to the previous nodes’ activations, then summing them with an added a bias. Later on, the node’s weights and bias will be tuned through training to more effectively recognize hidden connections within the data. From there, these nodes’ activations will be passed into additional hidden layers until the final layer is reached.



A neural network with multiple hidden layers


Finally, after all of the neurons in the hidden layers activate, the neural network will return a value in the output layer. Sometimes this value will manifest as a probability between which of multiple outcomes will most likely be observed, or as a single number that predicts some metric (such as life expectancy). It’s important to note that these are the model’s best guesses, and not the objective truth. This will give us the outputs that we’ll test for accuracy in the training phase.

title: A Beginner’s Guide to Understanding Neural Networks
text:
Training Process

Analyzing Loss
Naturally, nobody will perfectly set up a neural network on the first try. The connections between nodes are incredibly numerous and dense, so someone looking at a neural network’s connections could realistically only understand them as a black box. However, you can mechanically optimize a neural network through a process called gradient descent, where you pay attention to the model’s MSE (or some other loss function), then systematically adjust the linear combination of each node’s weights in the direction that will reduce the MSE the most. After enough iterations, the loss should be significantly diminished! \[
MSE = \text{mean}((w*x-y))^2
\]


Training, Validation, and Testing
We train a neural network by splitting our existing training data into training, validation, and testing sets. - The training set helps initialize node weights - The validation set gives out of sample checkpoints - The testing set is used at the end of training to test the network on ‘brand new data’
This method of training is vital to make sure that the model is not overfit on the training data and will be capable of working with real data.

title: A Beginner’s Guide to Understanding Neural Networks
text:
Example with MNIST Data
The MNIST database (Data:)is a massive database that consists of tens of thousands of handwritten numbers in a 28x28 pixel resolution that each come with classifying labels.



Example images from MNIST


This dataset is a classic for explaining the process of how neural networks function.
Since there are 784 pixels in a given 28x28 image, one would initialize the neural network with 784 neurons in the input layer. Additionally, since there are 10 numbers that the number could be, the neural network will have 10 output neurons that correspond to 0-9. The person setting up the neural network would also divide the data into a training, validation, and testing set, then would begin the training process.
Each input layer node will accept a number between 0.00 and 1.0 that represents the pixel’s grayscale as that input neuron’s activation.



Example MNIST input with pixel activations


From there, those inputs will be passed into the first hidden layer (whose number of neurons will depend on how the neural network is set up). Then, each node from the first hidden layer will act as the input for the next hidden layer, which will continue until the output layer is reached. The output layer node with the highest activation will be what the network classifies the number as.
From there, the neural network will figure out the total MSE between the output neurons and their classified labels (which will be 0 for all outputs except the correct label), then do some gradient descent to adjust the weights, then will see how those changes affect the MSE of a different input from the training set.
Finally, after enough rounds of training and validation, the model will be run with the test set to see how accurate it is with brand new data.

title: A Beginner’s Guide to Understanding Neural Networks
text:
Conclusion
I hope this has given you a better idea of how neural networks function and that the parallels to deep learning are clear (predictive inference, data-based training process, etc.) If you are interested in learning more, I’d recommend looking into training enhancements (like learning rates or dropout) or the math behind gradient descent!
